claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, pairing odor with food deprivation results in aversive olfactory learning.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, pairing odor with food deprivation results in aversive olfactory learning, and pairing odor with food results in appetitive learning.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, pairing odor with food results in appetitive learning.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, pairing odor with food deprivation results in aversive olfactory learning, and pairing odor with food results in appetitive learning.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aversive learning requires nuclear translocation of the cGMP-dependent protein kinase EGL-4 in AWC olfactory neurons.
source: Aversive learning requires nuclear translocation of the cGMP-dependent protein kinase EGL-4 in AWC olfactory neurons and an insulin signal from AIA interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and confirmed by experiments in this manuscript.

claim: Aversive learning requires an insulin signal from AIA interneurons.
source: Aversive learning requires nuclear translocation of the cGMP-dependent protein kinase EGL-4 in AWC olfactory neurons and an insulin signal from AIA interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and confirmed by experiments in this manuscript.

claim: The activity of neurons including AIA is acutely required during aversive, but not appetitive, learning.
source: Here we show that the activity of neurons including AIA is acutely required during aversive, but not appetitive, learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HisCl1 silencing experiments and unc-103(gf) experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The AIA circuit and AGE-1, an insulin-regulated PI3 kinase, signal to AWC to drive nuclear enrichment of EGL-4 during conditioning.
source: The AIA circuit and AGE-1, an insulin-regulated PI3 kinase, signal to AWC to drive nuclear enrichment of EGL-4 during conditioning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EGL-4::GFP localization experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Odor exposure shifts the AWC dynamic range to higher odor concentrations regardless of food pairing or the AIA circuit.
source: Odor exposure shifts the AWC dynamic range to higher odor concentrations regardless of food pairing or the AIA circuit, whereas AWC coupling to motor circuits is oppositely regulated by aversive and appetitive learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: AWC coupling to motor circuits is oppositely regulated by aversive and appetitive learning.
source: Odor exposure shifts the AWC dynamic range to higher odor concentrations regardless of food pairing or the AIA circuit, whereas AWC coupling to motor circuits is oppositely regulated by aversive and appetitive learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by channelrhodopsin experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Non-associative sensory adaptation in AWC encodes odor history.
source: These results suggest that non-associative sensory adaptation in AWC encodes odor history, while associative behavioral preference is encoded by altered AWC synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AWC dynamic range shifts occur regardless of food context.

claim: Associative behavioral preference is encoded by altered AWC synaptic activity.
source: These results suggest that non-associative sensory adaptation in AWC encodes odor history, while associative behavioral preference is encoded by altered AWC synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AWC-driven reversal behavior changes bidirectionally with food context.

claim: The retina adapts to ambient light levels over a 10^10-fold range.
source: Primary sensory neurons adjust their sensitivity and dynamic range to capture ongoing sensory information without saturating, a phenomenon illustrated by the adaptation of the retina to ambient light levels over a 1010-fold range (Arshavsky and Burns, 2012; Fain et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The nervous system of C. elegans is composed of 302 neurons.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, whose nervous system is composed of 302 neurons, shows robust plasticity in olfactory, mechanosensory, thermosensory, and gustatory behaviors (Colbert et al., 1995; Rankin, 1991; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Saeki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: C. elegans shows robust plasticity in olfactory, mechanosensory, thermosensory, and gustatory behaviors.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, whose nervous system is composed of 302 neurons, shows robust plasticity in olfactory, mechanosensory, thermosensory, and gustatory behaviors (Colbert et al., 1995; Rankin, 1991; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Saeki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans detects hundreds of volatile odors using dedicated sensory neurons.
source: C. elegans detects hundreds of volatile odors using dedicated sensory neurons, each of which expresses multiple G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Troemel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Each C. elegans olfactory neuron expresses multiple G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
source: C. elegans detects hundreds of volatile odors using dedicated sensory neurons, each of which expresses multiple G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Troemel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: AWCON detects benzaldehyde, butanone, and isoamyl alcohol.
source: For example, an olfactory neuron called AWCON (one of two AWC neurons) detects benzaldehyde, butanone, and isoamyl alcohol, and expresses at least five chemosensory GPCRs (Bargmann, 2006; Lesch and Bargmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AWCON expresses at least five chemosensory GPCRs.
source: For example, an olfactory neuron called AWCON (one of two AWC neurons) detects benzaldehyde, butanone, and isoamyl alcohol, and expresses at least five chemosensory GPCRs (Bargmann, 2006; Lesch and Bargmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AWC signal transduction resembles mammalian phototransduction.
source: Calcium imaging and genetic studies indicate that AWC signal transduction resembles mammalian phototransduction: odors are inferred to decrease the level of cGMP, close a cGMP-dependent transduction channel, and hyperpolarize AWC (Bargmann, 2006; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Odors decrease the level of cGMP in AWC.
source: Calcium imaging and genetic studies indicate that AWC signal transduction resembles mammalian phototransduction: odors are inferred to decrease the level of cGMP, close a cGMP-dependent transduction channel, and hyperpolarize AWC (Bargmann, 2006; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from calcium imaging and genetic studies cited.

claim: Odors close a cGMP-dependent transduction channel in AWC.
source: Calcium imaging and genetic studies indicate that AWC signal transduction resembles mammalian phototransduction: odors are inferred to decrease the level of cGMP, close a cGMP-dependent transduction channel, and hyperpolarize AWC (Bargmann, 2006; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from calcium imaging and genetic studies cited.

claim: Odors hyperpolarize AWC.
source: Calcium imaging and genetic studies indicate that AWC signal transduction resembles mammalian phototransduction: odors are inferred to decrease the level of cGMP, close a cGMP-dependent transduction channel, and hyperpolarize AWC (Bargmann, 2006; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from calcium imaging and genetic studies cited.

claim: When C. elegans is exposed to high concentrations of an odor in the absence of food, it gradually loses its attraction to that odor over an hour or more.
source: When C. elegans is exposed to high concentrations of an odor in the absence of food, it gradually loses its attraction to that odor over an hour or more, and recovers over a similar timescale (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: C. elegans recovers attraction to an odor over a similar timescale to the loss of attraction.
source: When C. elegans is exposed to high concentrations of an odor in the absence of food, it gradually loses its attraction to that odor over an hour or more, and recovers over a similar timescale (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Aversive olfactory learning requires pairing with food deprivation.
source: This process has been called adaptation, but will here be called aversive olfactory learning to reflect its long duration and the required pairing with food deprivation (Nuttley et al., 2002), and to distinguish it from short-term sensory adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Aversive learning is selective for the experienced odor, even when two odors are sensed by partly overlapping olfactory neurons.
source: Aversive learning is selective for the experienced odor, even when two odors are sensed by partly overlapping olfactory neurons (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The genetic requirements for aversive learning vary depending on the odor and the duration of odor exposure.
source: The genetic requirements for aversive learning vary depending on the odor and the duration of odor exposure, and include G protein signaling pathways, ion channels, and transcriptional regulators (Ardiel and Rankin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The genetic requirements for aversive learning include G protein signaling pathways, ion channels, and transcriptional regulators.
source: The genetic requirements for aversive learning vary depending on the odor and the duration of odor exposure, and include G protein signaling pathways, ion channels, and transcriptional regulators (Ardiel and Rankin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: egl-4 mutants show learning defects to multiple AWC-sensed odors.
source: egl-4 mutants show learning defects to multiple AWC-sensed odors, among other sensory defects (Daniels et al., 2000; L'Etoile et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After prolonged odor conditioning, EGL-4 translocates from the AWC cytoplasm to the nucleus.
source: After prolonged odor conditioning, EGL-4 translocates from the AWC cytoplasm to the nucleus (O'Halloran et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010), where it phosphorylates the heterochromatin protein HPL-2 and alters gene expression (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EGL-4 phosphorylates the heterochromatin protein HPL-2 in the nucleus.
source: After prolonged odor conditioning, EGL-4 translocates from the AWC cytoplasm to the nucleus (O'Halloran et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010), where it phosphorylates the heterochromatin protein HPL-2 and alters gene expression (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EGL-4 alters gene expression in the AWC nucleus.
source: After prolonged odor conditioning, EGL-4 translocates from the AWC cytoplasm to the nucleus (O'Halloran et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2010), where it phosphorylates the heterochromatin protein HPL-2 and alters gene expression (Juang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nuclear translocation of EGL-4 is a real-time marker for AWC plasticity.
source: Nuclear translocation of EGL-4 is a real-time marker for AWC plasticity (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EGL-4 translocation requires olfactory signal transduction and endogenous cGMP signaling in AWC.
source: EGL-4 translocation requires olfactory signal transduction and endogenous cGMP signaling in AWC, but exogenous cGMP is not sufficient to modify EGL-4 localization (O'Halloran et al., 2012﻿﻿), suggesting that a second coincident signal is required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Exogenous cGMP is not sufficient to modify EGL-4 localization.
source: EGL-4 translocation requires olfactory signal transduction and endogenous cGMP signaling in AWC, but exogenous cGMP is not sufficient to modify EGL-4 localization (O'Halloran et al., 2012﻿﻿), suggesting that a second coincident signal is required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A second coincident signal is required for EGL-4 translocation.
source: EGL-4 translocation requires olfactory signal transduction and endogenous cGMP signaling in AWC, but exogenous cGMP is not sufficient to modify EGL-4 localization (O'Halloran et al., 2012﻿﻿), suggesting that a second coincident signal is required.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that exogenous cGMP is insufficient.

claim: Aversive learning only occurs when odors are paired with food deprivation.
source: The existence of a coincident context signal for learning is further supported by the observation that aversive learning only occurs when odors are paired with food deprivation (Nuttley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Butanone odor becomes more attractive after pairing with food.
source: Indeed, butanone odor becomes more attractive after pairing with food, indicating that food context drives bidirectional olfactory learning (Torayama et al., 2007; Kauffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Food context drives bidirectional olfactory learning.
source: Indeed, butanone odor becomes more attractive after pairing with food, indicating that food context drives bidirectional olfactory learning (Torayama et al., 2007; Kauffmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that food pairing increases attraction while food deprivation decreases it.

claim: Aversive learning requires insulin signals from other neurons that feed back onto AWC and reduce its activity.
source: The integration of food context may involve communication between neurons, as aversive learning requires insulin signals from other neurons that feed back onto AWC and reduce its activity (Chalasani et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans is strongly attracted to butanone.
source: C. elegans is strongly attracted to butanone, an odor sensed by the AWCON olfactory neuron, but this attraction is lost after butanone is paired with food deprivation for 90 min (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the chemotaxis assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Butanone is sensed by the AWCON olfactory neuron.
source: C. elegans is strongly attracted to butanone, an odor sensed by the AWCON olfactory neuron, but this attraction is lost after butanone is paired with food deprivation for 90 min (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans olfaction.

claim: Attraction to butanone is lost after butanone is paired with food deprivation for 90 min.
source: C. elegans is strongly attracted to butanone, an odor sensed by the AWCON olfactory neuron, but this attraction is lost after butanone is paired with food deprivation for 90 min (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the chemotaxis assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Aversive learning in gcy-28d::HisCl1 animals exposed to histamine during conditioning is nearly eliminated.
source: Among a panel of tested strains, aversive learning was nearly eliminated in gcy-28d::HisCl1 animals that were exposed to histamine during conditioning (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral data in Figure 1C.

claim: The gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene is expressed reliably in AIA (100%) and AVF (90%) neurons.
source: This transgene is expressed reliably in AIA (100%) and AVF (90%) neurons and less frequently in ASI, I1, IL2 and M3 neurons (see Materials and methods); AIA and ASI form synapses with AWC.
evidence: This is determined by microscopic observation described in Materials and methods.

claim: The gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene is expressed less frequently in ASI, I1, IL2 and M3 neurons.
source: This transgene is expressed reliably in AIA (100%) and AVF (90%) neurons and less frequently in ASI, I1, IL2 and M3 neurons (see Materials and methods); AIA and ASI form synapses with AWC.
evidence: This is determined by microscopic observation described in Materials and methods.

claim: AIA and ASI form synapses with AWC.
source: This transgene is expressed reliably in AIA (100%) and AVF (90%) neurons and less frequently in ASI, I1, IL2 and M3 neurons (see Materials and methods); AIA and ASI form synapses with AWC.
evidence: This is based on the C. elegans wiring diagram.

claim: Histamine does not affect butanone chemotaxis in wild-type animals.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that histamine did not affect butanone chemotaxis or aversive learning in wild-type animals, and that the HisCl1 transgenes were innocuous in the absence of histamine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Histamine does not affect aversive learning in wild-type animals.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that histamine did not affect butanone chemotaxis or aversive learning in wild-type animals, and that the HisCl1 transgenes were innocuous in the absence of histamine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The HisCl1 transgenes are innocuous in the absence of histamine.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that histamine did not affect butanone chemotaxis or aversive learning in wild-type animals, and that the HisCl1 transgenes were innocuous in the absence of histamine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: gcy-28d::HisCl1 selectively silences neurons required during the conditioning period for aversive olfactory learning.
source: Thus gcy-28d::HisCl1 selectively silences neurons required during the conditioning period for aversive olfactory learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that silencing with histamine during conditioning eliminates learning.

claim: An unc-4::HisCl1 transgene that is expressed in AVF caused a partial learning defect.
source: The most promising initial candidate in the gcy-28d set was AVF, because an unc-4::HisCl1 transgene that is expressed in AVF caused a partial learning defect (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1C.

claim: unc-4::HisCl1 is expressed in many neurons other than AVF.
source: However, unc-4::HisCl1 is expressed in many neurons other than AVF that might contribute to its effect.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of unc-4 promoter expression pattern.

claim: dsRNA-induced silencing of the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AVF did not rescue aversive learning.
source: Moreover, dsRNA-induced silencing of the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AVF did not rescue aversive learning, but instead caused a mild chemotaxis defect (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1D.

claim: dsRNA-induced silencing of the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AVF caused a mild chemotaxis defect.
source: Moreover, dsRNA-induced silencing of the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AVF did not rescue aversive learning, but instead caused a mild chemotaxis defect (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1D.

claim: AVF might affect chemotaxis rather than learning per se.
source: These results suggest that AVF might affect chemotaxis rather than learning per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that silencing AVF causes chemotaxis defects but doesn't rescue learning.

claim: Silencing the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AIA consistently restored aversive learning.
source: Silencing the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AIA consistently restored aversive learning (Figure 1D), a result that implicates AIA in learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1D.

claim: AIA is implicated in learning.
source: Silencing the gcy-28d::HisCl1 transgene in AIA consistently restored aversive learning (Figure 1D), a result that implicates AIA in learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of learning when AIA is not silenced.

claim: Silencing AIA alone with HisCl1 did not disrupt learning.
source: However, silencing AIA alone or in several combinations with other neurons with HisCl1 did not disrupt learning (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1C.

claim: Simultaneous silencing of AIA and at least one unidentified neuron cause the aversive learning defect in the gcy-28d::HisCl1 strain.
source: These results suggest that simultaneous silencing of AIA and at least one unidentified neuron cause the aversive learning defect in the gcy-28d::HisCl1 strain.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results with different silencing combinations.

claim: Expressing an overactive UNC-103 potassium channel under the gcy-28d promoter resulted in a strong defect in aversive olfactory learning.
source: As an alternative chronic silencing method, we expressed an overactive UNC-103 potassium channel under the gcy-28d promoter. This transgene resulted in a strong defect in aversive olfactory learning (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1E.

claim: The gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene is expressed reliably in AIA interneurons.
source: The gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene is expressed reliably in AIA interneurons and only occasionally in other neurons (see Materials and methods), supporting the hypothesis that AIA promotes aversive learning.
evidence: This is determined by microscopic observation described in Materials and methods.

claim: The gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene is expressed only occasionally in neurons other than AIA.
source: The gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene is expressed reliably in AIA interneurons and only occasionally in other neurons (see Materials and methods), supporting the hypothesis that AIA promotes aversive learning.
evidence: This is determined by microscopic observation described in Materials and methods.

claim: AIA promotes aversive learning.
source: The gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene is expressed reliably in AIA interneurons and only occasionally in other neurons (see Materials and methods), supporting the hypothesis that AIA promotes aversive learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the learning defect when AIA is silenced.

claim: Appetitive olfactory learning was unaffected by silencing the AIA circuit with the gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene.
source: Appetitive olfactory learning was unaffected by silencing the AIA circuit with the gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene (Figure 1F), indicating a preferential requirement for the AIA circuit in aversive learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a preferential requirement for the AIA circuit in aversive learning.
source: Appetitive olfactory learning was unaffected by silencing the AIA circuit with the gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) transgene (Figure 1F), indicating a preferential requirement for the AIA circuit in aversive learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect on aversive but not appetitive learning.

claim: Retrograde insulin (ins-1) signaling from AIA to AWC is implicated in aversive learning to odors including benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol.
source: The AIA interneurons receive synaptic input from numerous chemosensory neurons, and make reciprocal synapses onto a few, including AWC. Previous studies have implicated retrograde insulin (ins-1) signaling from AIA to AWC in aversive learning to odors including benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol (Lin et al., 2010; Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Aversive learning to butanone was lost in the ins-1 mutant.
source: We found that aversive learning to butanone was also lost in the ins-1 mutant, and was rescued by expressing ins-1 in the AIA neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Aversive learning to butanone was rescued by expressing ins-1 in the AIA neurons.
source: We found that aversive learning to butanone was also lost in the ins-1 mutant, and was rescued by expressing ins-1 in the AIA neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: INS-1 and other insulin-like proteins act on the insulin receptor DAF-2.
source: INS-1 and other insulin-like proteins act on the insulin receptor DAF-2, which regulates the AGE-1 phosphatidyl inositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and downstream kinases and transcription factors (Murphy and Hu, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DAF-2 regulates the AGE-1 phosphatidyl inositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and downstream kinases and transcription factors.
source: INS-1 and other insulin-like proteins act on the insulin receptor DAF-2, which regulates the AGE-1 phosphatidyl inositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and downstream kinases and transcription factors (Murphy and Hu, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: daf-2 null mutants are inviable.
source: daf-2 and age-1 null mutants are inviable, but viable age-1 reduction of function mutants were defective in aversive olfactory learning, and could be rescued by expressing age-1 in AWCON (Figure 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants.

claim: age-1 null mutants are inviable.
source: daf-2 and age-1 null mutants are inviable, but viable age-1 reduction of function mutants were defective in aversive olfactory learning, and could be rescued by expressing age-1 in AWCON (Figure 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants.

claim: Viable age-1 reduction of function mutants were defective in aversive olfactory learning.
source: daf-2 and age-1 null mutants are inviable, but viable age-1 reduction of function mutants were defective in aversive olfactory learning, and could be rescued by expressing age-1 in AWCON (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: The aversive learning defect in age-1 mutants could be rescued by expressing age-1 in AWCON.
source: daf-2 and age-1 null mutants are inviable, but viable age-1 reduction of function mutants were defective in aversive olfactory learning, and could be rescued by expressing age-1 in AWCON (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Insulin signaling to AWC is one possible mechanism by which the AIA circuit could regulate aversive learning to butanone.
source: Thus insulin signaling to AWC is one possible mechanism by which the AIA circuit could regulate aversive learning to butanone.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Odor conditioning led to enrichment of EGL-4::GFP in the AWC nucleus within 90 min.
source: In agreement with previous results, odor conditioning led to enrichment of EGL-4::GFP in the AWC nucleus within 90 min (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data in Figure 3B.

claim: When the AIA circuit was silenced, naive and butanone-conditioned animals had indistinguishable EGL-4::GFP localization in AWC.
source: However, when the AIA circuit was silenced, naive and butanone-conditioned animals had indistinguishable EGL-4::GFP localization in AWC, resembling naive wild-type animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data in Figure 3C.

claim: Nuclear enrichment of EGL-4::GFP is a cell-biological readout of signaling from the AIA circuit to AWC.
source: These results identify nuclear enrichment of EGL-4::GFP as a cell-biological readout of signaling from the AIA circuit to AWC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AIA silencing prevents EGL-4 translocation.

claim: age-1 (PI3K) reduction of function mutants failed to relocalize EGL-4::GFP in AWC after odor conditioning.
source: Indeed, age-1 (PI3K) reduction of function mutants, which were defective in aversive learning (Figure 2), also failed to relocalize EGL-4::GFP in AWC after odor conditioning (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data in Figure 3D.

claim: Attractive odors reduce AWCON calcium.
source: Attractive odors reduce AWCON calcium, and subsequent odor removal results in a calcium increase that can overshoot before returning to baseline (Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Odor removal results in a calcium increase in AWCON that can overshoot before returning to baseline.
source: Attractive odors reduce AWCON calcium, and subsequent odor removal results in a calcium increase that can overshoot before returning to baseline (Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A near-complete loss of AWC odor sensitivity occurs after an hour of conditioning with isoamyl alcohol.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated a near-complete loss of AWC odor sensitivity after an hour of conditioning with isoamyl alcohol (Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: AWCON calcium responses at 1 µM butanone were greatly diminished after butanone conditioning.
source: Using genetically-encoded calcium indicators to monitor butanone responses after aversive learning, we found that AWCON calcium responses at 1 µM butanone were greatly diminished after butanone conditioning (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: AWCON responses were restored after ten minutes of recovery in buffer.
source: However, the AWCON responses were restored after ten minutes of recovery in buffer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: Short-term suppression of butanone responses appears insufficient to explain aversive learning behavior, which persists through an hour-long chemotaxis assay.
source: This short-term suppression of butanone responses appears insufficient to explain aversive learning behavior, which persists through an hour-long chemotaxis assay (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of recovery time and behavioral persistence.

claim: AWCON calcium is suppressed by butanone over a 10^5-fold concentration range from 11 nM to 1 mM.
source: A dose-response curve of naive animals showed that AWCON calcium is suppressed by butanone over a 105-fold concentration range from 11 nM to 1 mM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B.

claim: Suppression of basal calcium by odor saturated between 111 nM and 1 µM butanone.
source: This suppression of basal calcium by odor saturated between 111 nM and 1 µM butanone, was followed by a significant calcium overshoot after odor removal at 11 nM to 11 µM, and recovered to baseline only slowly from odor concentrations above 11 µM (Figure 4B–D, black traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: A significant calcium overshoot after odor removal occurs at 11 nM to 11 µM butanone.
source: This suppression of basal calcium by odor saturated between 111 nM and 1 µM butanone, was followed by a significant calcium overshoot after odor removal at 11 nM to 11 µM, and recovered to baseline only slowly from odor concentrations above 11 µM (Figure 4B–D, black traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: AWCON recovered to baseline only slowly from odor concentrations above 11 µM.
source: This suppression of basal calcium by odor saturated between 111 nM and 1 µM butanone, was followed by a significant calcium overshoot after odor removal at 11 nM to 11 µM, and recovered to baseline only slowly from odor concentrations above 11 µM (Figure 4B–D, black traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: After butanone conditioning, the dynamic range of AWCON calcium responses was shifted toward higher concentrations.
source: After pairing butanone conditioning with food deprivation, the dynamic range of AWCON calcium responses was shifted toward higher concentrations (Figure 4B,C; red traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the detection threshold.
source: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the detection threshold, a ten-fold increase in the saturation concentration, a faster recovery after odor removal, and a reduced calcium overshoot compared to control animals conditioned in buffer alone (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the saturation concentration.
source: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the detection threshold, a ten-fold increase in the saturation concentration, a faster recovery after odor removal, and a reduced calcium overshoot compared to control animals conditioned in buffer alone (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Butanone-conditioned animals had a faster recovery after odor removal.
source: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the detection threshold, a ten-fold increase in the saturation concentration, a faster recovery after odor removal, and a reduced calcium overshoot compared to control animals conditioned in buffer alone (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Butanone-conditioned animals had a reduced calcium overshoot compared to control animals.
source: Butanone-conditioned animals had a ten-fold increase in the detection threshold, a ten-fold increase in the saturation concentration, a faster recovery after odor removal, and a reduced calcium overshoot compared to control animals conditioned in buffer alone (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The shift in dynamic range persisted for at least 40 min.
source: The shift in dynamic range persisted for at least 40 min, consistent with the time course of aversive learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Naive AWCON calcium responses in gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) strain resembled those of wild-type animals.
source: Naive AWCON calcium responses in this strain resembled those of wild-type animals (Figure 5A, black traces).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5A.

claim: Butanone conditioning in gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) resulted in the same shift in the AWCON threshold, saturation concentration, and recovery dynamics as in the wild type.
source: Surprisingly, butanone conditioning resulted in the same shift in the AWCON threshold, saturation concentration, and recovery dynamics as in the wild type (Figure 5A–C, red traces), despite the fact that these animals did not show aversive learning at a behavioral level.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The shift in AWCON dynamic range after conditioning is not sufficient for learning.
source: This result demonstrates that the shift in AWCON dynamic range after conditioning is not sufficient for learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the shift occurs without behavioral learning in gcy-28d::unc-103(gf).

claim: The AWCON dynamic range also shifted after butanone conditioning in age-1 PI3K mutants.
source: The AWCON dynamic range also shifted after butanone conditioning in age-1 PI3K mutants, which have a learning defect (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Conditioned age-1 mutants had pronounced AWCON oscillations after odor removal.
source: In addition, conditioned age-1 mutants had pronounced AWCON oscillations after odor removal, as previously reported for ins-1 mutants (Figure 5—Source data 1; Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Behavioral attraction to butanone is enhanced after butanone is paired with food.
source: Behavioral attraction to butanone is enhanced after butanone is paired with food (Figure 1F), but AWCON was less sensitive to butanone in these conditioned animals than in the matched naive control (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 1F.

claim: AWCON was less sensitive to butanone after appetitive conditioning than in the matched naive control.
source: Behavioral attraction to butanone is enhanced after butanone is paired with food (Figure 1F), but AWCON was less sensitive to butanone in these conditioned animals than in the matched naive control (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5G-I.

claim: The AWCON calcium response was similarly affected by appetitive and aversive conditioning.
source: Indeed, the AWCON calcium response was similarly affected by appetitive and aversive conditioning, with a ten-fold increase in detection threshold, an increase in the saturation concentration, and a faster recovery after odor removal compared to naive controls (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 5H,I.

claim: The shift in butanone dynamic range in AWCON represents sensory adaptation to odor history, and not odor preference.
source: Thus the shift in butanone dynamic range in AWCON represents sensory adaptation to odor history, and not odor preference.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the shift occurs with both appetitive and aversive conditioning.

claim: Food deprivation alters AWCON responses.
source: This experiment also revealed that food deprivation alters AWCON responses: food-deprived naive animals (Figure 4B,C) detected lower butanone concentrations than well-fed naive animals (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing calcium imaging data from different feeding conditions.

claim: Food-deprived naive animals detected lower butanone concentrations than well-fed naive animals.
source: This experiment also revealed that food deprivation alters AWCON responses: food-deprived naive animals (Figure 4B,C) detected lower butanone concentrations than well-fed naive animals (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing calcium imaging data in Figures 4B,C and 5G,H.

claim: The calcium-calmodulin dependent protein kinase CMK-1 is a candidate to mediate the change in odor sensitivity due to food deprivation.
source: The calcium-calmodulin dependent protein kinase CMK-1, which shuttles between the AWC nucleus and cytoplasm in response to food deprivation, is a candidate to mediate this change in odor sensitivity (Neal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative, based on known properties of CMK-1 from cited work.

claim: CMK-1 shuttles between the AWC nucleus and cytoplasm in response to food deprivation.
source: The calcium-calmodulin dependent protein kinase CMK-1, which shuttles between the AWC nucleus and cytoplasm in response to food deprivation, is a candidate to mediate this change in odor sensitivity (Neal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: C. elegans locomotion alternates between forward runs and reversals.
source: C. elegans locomotion alternates between forward runs and reversals, which are regulated by odors during chemotaxis (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Iino and Yoshida, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reversals are regulated by odors during chemotaxis.
source: C. elegans locomotion alternates between forward runs and reversals, which are regulated by odors during chemotaxis (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Iino and Yoshida, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Odor removal increases AWCON activity and the frequency of reversals in wild-type animals.
source: Odor removal increases AWCON activity and the frequency of reversals in wild-type animals, but not in chemotaxis-defective mutants, suggesting that the acute reversal assay and chemotaxis are related (Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The acute reversal assay and chemotaxis are related.
source: Odor removal increases AWCON activity and the frequency of reversals in wild-type animals, but not in chemotaxis-defective mutants, suggesting that the acute reversal assay and chemotaxis are related (Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chemotaxis-defective mutants don't show the reversal response.

claim: Direct activation of AWCON with Channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR2) elicits reversals.
source: Like odor removal, direct activation of AWCON with the light-activated ion channel Channelrhodopsin 2 (ChR2) elicits reversals (Gordus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: AWCON::ChR2 bypasses odor transduction to depolarize AWC directly.
source: AWCON::ChR2 bypasses odor transduction to depolarize AWC directly, thereby separating AWC sensory processing from AWC coupling to behavioral circuits.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how channelrhodopsin works.

claim: Naive animals responded to AWCON activation with an increase in reversals.
source: Naive animals responded to AWCON activation with an increase in reversals, as previously reported (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6A,B and supported by citation.

claim: Butanone-conditioned animals did not reverse in response to AWCON::ChR2 stimulation.
source: By contrast, butanone-conditioned animals did not reverse in response to AWCON::ChR2 stimulation (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Aversive conditioning depresses AWCON coupling to target neurons that drive reversal behaviors.
source: This result suggests that aversive conditioning depresses AWCON coupling to target neurons that drive reversal behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of reversal response to AWCON stimulation after conditioning.

claim: Suppression of the AWCON::ChR2 response required the AIA circuit.
source: Suppression of the AWCON::ChR2 response required the AIA circuit, as gcy-28d::unc-103(gf) animals responded equally strongly to AWCON::ChR2 stimulation with or without butanone conditioning (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The behavioral response to AWCON::ChR2 stimulation in age-1 mutants was not significantly altered by conditioning.
source: Similarly, the behavioral response to AWCON::ChR2 stimulation in age-1 mutants was not significantly altered by conditioning, matching their failure in aversive learning (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6E,F.

claim: After butanone was paired with food, AWCON::ChR2 stimulation elicited a substantially greater increase in reversals than it did in naive controls.
source: Finally, we tested the effects of appetitive conditioning on AWC output using the same assay. After butanone was paired with food, AWCON::ChR2 stimulation elicited a substantially greater increase in reversals than it did in naive controls (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6G,H.

claim: AWCON::ChR2-driven behavioral output demonstrates bidirectional plasticity after conditioning that mirrors aversive and appetitive learning behaviors.
source: Therefore, AWCON::ChR2-driven behavioral output demonstrates bidirectional plasticity after conditioning that mirrors aversive and appetitive learning behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite effects of aversive and appetitive conditioning on reversal responses.

claim: Odor conditioning alters the coupling of AWC to motor circuits.
source: These results indicate that odor conditioning alters the coupling of AWC to motor circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the changes in behavioral output after conditioning.

claim: AIB is an interneuron that receives direct and indirect synaptic output from AWC.
source: To narrow down the locus at which this change might occur, we examined AIB, an interneuron that receives direct and indirect synaptic output from AWC.
evidence: This is based on the C. elegans wiring diagram.

claim: Channelrhodopsin activation of AIB elicits reversals in naive animals.
source: Channelrhodopsin activation of AIB elicits reversals in naive animals, like activation of AWC (Gordus et al., 2015; Piggott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AIB::ChR2 illumination elicited reversals equally well in naive and butanone-conditioned animals.
source: AIB::ChR2 illumination elicited reversals equally well in naive and butanone-conditioned animals, localizing plasticity to a site upstream of or parallel to AIB (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data in Figure 6I,J.

claim: Plasticity is localized to a site upstream of or parallel to AIB.
source: AIB::ChR2 illumination elicited reversals equally well in naive and butanone-conditioned animals, localizing plasticity to a site upstream of or parallel to AIB (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AIB stimulation is unaffected by conditioning.

claim: Butanone conditioning modifies two aspects of AWCON function.
source: Butanone conditioning modifies two aspects of AWCON function (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The dynamic range of AWCON calcium signaling shifts toward higher butanone concentrations after conditioning.
source: First, the dynamic range of AWCON calcium signaling shifts toward higher butanone concentrations after conditioning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The alteration in AWCON dynamic range is equivalently induced by aversive and appetitive conditioning.
source: This alteration in AWCON is equivalently induced by aversive and appetitive conditioning, indicating that AWC sensitivity is a non-associative representation of odor history.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments comparing aversive and appetitive conditioning.

claim: AWC sensitivity is a non-associative representation of odor history.
source: This alteration in AWCON is equivalently induced by aversive and appetitive conditioning, indicating that AWC sensitivity is a non-associative representation of odor history.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the shift occurs regardless of food context.

claim: The coupling of AWCON activity with reversal behavior decreases after odor is paired with food deprivation.
source: Second, the coupling of AWCON activity with reversal behavior decreases after odor is paired with food deprivation, and increases after odor is paired with food.
evidence: This is demonstrated by channelrhodopsin experiments.

claim: The coupling of AWCON activity with reversal behavior increases after odor is paired with food.
source: Second, the coupling of AWCON activity with reversal behavior decreases after odor is paired with food deprivation, and increases after odor is paired with food.
evidence: This is demonstrated by channelrhodopsin experiments.

claim: Bidirectional plasticity in AWCON coupling is associative.
source: This bidirectional plasticity is associative; it integrates odor experience with food context and mirrors the behavioral preference after learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the dependence on food context and correlation with behavior.

claim: Bidirectional plasticity in AWCON coupling integrates odor experience with food context.
source: This bidirectional plasticity is associative; it integrates odor experience with food context and mirrors the behavioral preference after learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for both odor and food context.

claim: Bidirectional plasticity in AWCON coupling mirrors the behavioral preference after learning.
source: This bidirectional plasticity is associative; it integrates odor experience with food context and mirrors the behavioral preference after learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between AWCON output changes and behavioral changes.

claim: Silencing AIA and other gcy-28d-expressing neurons acutely during conditioning prevents aversive learning.
source: Silencing AIA and other gcy-28d-expressing neurons acutely during conditioning prevents aversive learning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HisCl1 silencing experiments.

claim: The relevant neurons silenced by gcy-28d::HisCl1 might include ASI.
source: In addition to AIA, the relevant neurons might include ASI, which expresses ins-1 and has redundant roles with AIA in aversive learning to benzaldehyde (Lin et al., 2010), and AVF, a little-characterized neuron with a role in locomotion (Hardaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is speculative, based on expression patterns and prior work.

claim: ASI expresses ins-1.
source: In addition to AIA, the relevant neurons might include ASI, which expresses ins-1 and has redundant roles with AIA in aversive learning to benzaldehyde (Lin et al., 2010), and AVF, a little-characterized neuron with a role in locomotion (Hardaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ASI has redundant roles with AIA in aversive learning to benzaldehyde.
source: In addition to AIA, the relevant neurons might include ASI, which expresses ins-1 and has redundant roles with AIA in aversive learning to benzaldehyde (Lin et al., 2010), and AVF, a little-characterized neuron with a role in locomotion (Hardaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: AVF has a role in locomotion.
source: In addition to AIA, the relevant neurons might include ASI, which expresses ins-1 and has redundant roles with AIA in aversive learning to benzaldehyde (Lin et al., 2010), and AVF, a little-characterized neuron with a role in locomotion (Hardaker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effects of the AIA circuit on aversive learning are similar to those of the insulin-like peptide ins-1.
source: The effects of the AIA circuit on aversive learning are similar to those of the insulin-like peptide ins-1, which is expressed in AIA, ASI, and other neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar behavioral and molecular phenotypes.

claim: ins-1 is expressed in AIA, ASI, and other neurons.
source: The effects of the AIA circuit on aversive learning are similar to those of the insulin-like peptide ins-1, which is expressed in AIA, ASI, and other neurons.
evidence: This is based on known expression patterns.

claim: The AIA circuit and insulin/PI3 kinase signaling have similar effects on nuclear translocation of EGL-4 in AWCON.
source: As well as having similar behavioral effects, the AIA circuit and insulin/PI3 kinase signaling have similar effects on nuclear translocation of EGL-4 in AWCON, which is essential for aversive learning (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EGL-4 localization experiments.

claim: Nuclear translocation of EGL-4 in AWCON is essential for aversive learning.
source: As well as having similar behavioral effects, the AIA circuit and insulin/PI3 kinase signaling have similar effects on nuclear translocation of EGL-4 in AWCON, which is essential for aversive learning (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: INS-1 and downstream PI3 kinase signaling have been implicated in retrograde signaling from AIA to sensory neurons in salt chemotaxis learning and benzaldehyde associative plasticity.
source: INS-1 and downstream PI3 kinase signaling have previously been implicated in retrograde signaling from AIA to sensory neurons in several behavioral paradigms including salt chemotaxis learning and benzaldehyde associative plasticity (Tomioka et al., 2006; Lin et al., 2010; Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: INS-1 is one of over 40 insulin-like peptides that may be agonists or antagonists of the insulin receptor DAF-2.
source: INS-1 is one of over 40 insulin-like peptides that may be agonists or antagonists of the insulin receptor DAF-2 (Murphy and Hu 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: INS-1 may not be unique in its ability to regulate aversive learning.
source: Given this diversity, INS-1 may not be unique in its ability to regulate aversive learning; under other circumstances, the PI3 kinase pathway in AWC could respond to other insulins secreted from other cells.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the diversity of insulin-like peptides.

claim: In Drosophila odor learning, olfactory CS information converges with electric shock or sucrose reward US information in the mushroom bodies.
source: In Drosophila odor learning, olfactory CS information converges with electric shock or sucrose reward US information in the mushroom bodies (Waddell, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In rodents, auditory CS information converges with electric shock US information in the amygdala.
source: In rodents, auditory CS information converges with electric shock US information in the amygdala (Romanski et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In Aplysia, classical conditioning pairs an electric shock US with a gentle tactile CS to strengthen synapses of the tactile CS sensory neurons.
source: In Aplysia, classical conditioning pairs an electric shock US with a gentle tactile CS to strengthen synapses of the tactile CS sensory neurons (Hawkins et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the visually-mediated ciliary response of Hermissenda, CS and US pathways converge at two sites – first-order interneurons shared by the two pathways, and sensory neurons of the CS pathway.
source: In the visually-mediated ciliary response of Hermissenda, CS and US pathways converge at two sites – first-order interneurons shared by the two pathways, and sensory neurons of the CS pathway (Crow and Tian, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In butanone plasticity of C. elegans, the odor is analogous to the CS.
source: In butanone plasticity of C. elegans, the odor is analogous to the CS, while the food or food deprivation context could be considered the US.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on classical conditioning framework.

claim: In butanone plasticity of C. elegans, the food or food deprivation context could be considered the US.
source: In butanone plasticity of C. elegans, the odor is analogous to the CS, while the food or food deprivation context could be considered the US.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on classical conditioning framework.

claim: Learning is specific to the conditioned odor.
source: Learning is specific to the conditioned odor, as expected for a classical CS (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The AIA circuit senses food deprivation.
source: We suggest that the AIA circuit senses food deprivation, and retrograde signaling to AWC merges this US information with odor-specific CS information.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the requirement for AIA in aversive learning.

claim: Retrograde signaling from the AIA circuit to AWC merges US information with odor-specific CS information.
source: We suggest that the AIA circuit senses food deprivation, and retrograde signaling to AWC merges this US information with odor-specific CS information.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the circuit analysis.

claim: The AIM neurons are implicated in long-term appetitive learning.
source: The AIM neurons that are implicated in long-term appetitive learning might have corresponding roles in encoding food as an appetitive US (Lakhina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative, based on citation to prior work.

claim: Organisms ranging from bacteria to mammals modify the sensitivity and dynamic range of sensory transduction after prolonged stimulation.
source: Organisms ranging from bacteria to mammals modify the sensitivity and dynamic range of sensory transduction after prolonged stimulation (Fain et al., 2001; Sourjik, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A strong but transient suppression of calcium responses occurs immediately after odor conditioning in AWCON.
source: In AWCON, we observed a strong but transient suppression of calcium responses immediately after odor conditioning (Chalasani et al., 2010), followed by a sustained shift in the sensitivity and dynamic range of the odor response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging and supported by citation.

claim: A sustained shift in the sensitivity and dynamic range of the odor response follows the transient suppression in AWCON.
source: In AWCON, we observed a strong but transient suppression of calcium responses immediately after odor conditioning (Chalasani et al., 2010), followed by a sustained shift in the sensitivity and dynamic range of the odor response.
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The change in AWCON dynamic range represents sensory adaptation to the average odor intensity in the animal's environment.
source: Aversive and appetitive conditioning elicited similar changes favoring higher odor concentrations, suggesting that this change represents sensory adaptation to the average odor intensity in the animal's environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of changes across different food contexts.

claim: The shift in AWCON dynamic range after odor conditioning may prevent saturation at higher odor concentrations.
source: The shift in AWCON dynamic range after odor conditioning may prevent saturation at higher odor concentrations, allowing detection of increasing odor concentrations against an odor background.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the functional interpretation of the shift.

claim: The increased butanone attraction after appetitive conditioning is most striking at high odor concentrations.
source: Indeed, the increased butanone attraction after appetitive conditioning is most striking at high odor concentrations (Torayama et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Naive animals are only weakly attracted to high butanone concentrations.
source: Naive animals are only weakly attracted to these concentrations, perhaps reflecting the saturation of their AWCON calcium response.
evidence: This is inferred from behavioral and calcium imaging data.

claim: After aversive conditioning, the AWCON neuron has a diminished ability to drive reversal behavior.
source: After aversive conditioning, the AWCON neuron has a diminished ability to drive reversal behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by channelrhodopsin experiments.

claim: The diminished ability of AWCON to drive reversals results from alterations in synaptic vesicle release by AWCON.
source: We suggest that this results from alterations in synaptic vesicle release by AWCON, which contains both glutamatergic and peptidergic vesicles (Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative, based on known properties of AWCON.

claim: AWCON contains both glutamatergic and peptidergic vesicles.
source: We suggest that this results from alterations in synaptic vesicle release by AWCON, which contains both glutamatergic and peptidergic vesicles (Chalasani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity include changes in the composition or level of the neuropeptides produced by AWC.
source: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity are changes in the composition or level of the neuropeptides produced by AWC, changes in the relative rates of release of the two vesicle classes, or changes in resting potential that affect basal neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms.

claim: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity include changes in the relative rates of release of the two vesicle classes.
source: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity are changes in the composition or level of the neuropeptides produced by AWC, changes in the relative rates of release of the two vesicle classes, or changes in resting potential that affect basal neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms.

claim: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity include changes in resting potential that affect basal neurotransmitter release.
source: Candidate mechanisms for plasticity are changes in the composition or level of the neuropeptides produced by AWC, changes in the relative rates of release of the two vesicle classes, or changes in resting potential that affect basal neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is speculative, proposing possible mechanisms.

claim: Gene expression changes induced by nuclear EGL-4 or other transcriptional regulators may contribute to functional effects on AWC output.
source: Gene expression changes induced by nuclear EGL-4 or other transcriptional regulators may contribute to these functional effects (Juang et al., 2013; Neal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative, based on citations to prior work.

claim: Sensory neuron synapses and related signaling pathways contribute to gustatory learning in C. elegans.
source: Sensory neuron synapses and related signaling pathways also contribute to gustatory learning in C. elegans.
evidence: This is supported by the discussion of salt learning below.

claim: C. elegans migrates to salt concentrations that have been paired with food.
source: C. elegans migrates to salt concentrations that have been paired with food (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014), and learns the association over about 90 min, a time frame similar to that of olfactory learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans learns the salt-food association over about 90 min.
source: C. elegans migrates to salt concentrations that have been paired with food (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014), and learns the association over about 90 min, a time frame similar to that of olfactory learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Salt preference changes are accompanied by synaptic changes in the ASER gustatory neuron that are induced by INS-1, AGE-1, and an axonal isoform of the DAF-2 insulin receptor.
source: Salt preference changes are accompanied by synaptic changes in the ASER gustatory neuron that are induced by INS-1, AGE-1, and an axonal isoform of the DAF-2 insulin receptor (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Oda et al., 2011; Ohno et al., 2014; Tomioka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bidirectional changes in ASER behavioral output below and above the preferred salt concentration are observed in a channelrhodopsin experiment.
source: Bidirectional changes in ASER behavioral output below and above the preferred salt concentration are observed in a channelrhodopsin experiment similar to the one reported here for AWCON (Kunitomo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Salt preference learning is accompanied by bidirectional shifts in the salt concentration that activates ASER in calcium imaging experiments.
source: Unlike olfactory learning, however, salt preference learning is accompanied by bidirectional shifts in the salt concentration that activates ASER in calcium imaging experiments (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans temperature preference learning results in precise bidirectional shifts in the temperature sensitivity of the AFD thermosensory neurons.
source: Similarly, C. elegans temperature preference learning results in precise bidirectional shifts in the temperature sensitivity of the AFD thermosensory neurons (Kimura et al., 2004; Clark et al., 2006; Ramot et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In thermotaxis and gustatory plasticity, animals seek out a preferred concentration at the 'setpoint', the temperature or salt condition associated with chronic cultivation.
source: In thermotaxis and gustatory plasticity, animals seek out a preferred concentration at the 'setpoint', the temperature or salt condition associated with chronic cultivation (Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Olfactory plasticity is relatively insensitive to setpoint.
source: Olfactory plasticity, by contrast, is relatively insensitive to setpoint.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with thermotaxis and gustatory plasticity.

claim: Olfactory plasticity is linked to the identity of the odor, not the quantity.
source: It is linked to the identity of the odor, not the quantity, and the readouts of aversive and appetitive learning are observed across 100-fold concentration changes in the odor source (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Torayama et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The readouts of aversive and appetitive learning are observed across 100-fold concentration changes in the odor source.
source: It is linked to the identity of the odor, not the quantity, and the readouts of aversive and appetitive learning are observed across 100-fold concentration changes in the odor source (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Torayama et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In olfactory learning, it is the context-dependent synaptic changes that appear to be instructive for behavioral preference.
source: Although odor history does change sensory representations in AWCON, this is not central to the behavioral preference; it is the context-dependent synaptic changes that appear to be instructive.
evidence: This is inferred from the dissociation of sensory adaptation and behavioral preference.
